senses.gloss:
caitanya
(‘consciousness’)
------------------------------------------
In the Indian philosophical systems, the word has been used widely to denote चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. Some systems like the Vedānta, identify it with the आत्मन्/ ब्रह्मन्.
The Cārvākas (materialists) who admit of only four bhūtas or fundamental elements consider चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् as the property of the body and a product of these elements, like the intoxicating power of a drink being produced by the chemical combination of certain things. The न्याय and Vaiśeṣika schools consider it as a quality of the सोउल् produced in it by its conjunction with the मिन्द् and other conditions of knowledge. The Mīmāṁsakas and Jainas also hold the same view. The Buddhist schools consider it as a series of momentary cognitions, each revealing itself. But Sāṅkhya, योग and Advaita Vedānta systems consider it as the very nature of the सोउल्, knowledge being only a manifestation or reflection of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् on the vṛttis or modifications of the मिन्द्.
These schools usually recognize three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्: जाग्रत् or waking state, स्वप्न or dream state and सुषुप्ति or deep-sleep state. In the waking state knowledge is produced by the contact of the sense-organs with the sense-objects. In the dream state it is produced through सṁस्कारस् or past impressions, eventhough there is no contact between the senses and the objects. In the deep-sleep state, some schools like the न्याय aver that there is no knowledge whereas the Sāṅkhya, योग and Vedānta schools accept the existence of a subtle kind of knowledge, a knowledge about the तमस् or nescience which prevails at that time.
In some of the monastic orders of the Daśanāmī group, this word ‘caitanya’ is used as an appellation to indicate the state of a ब्रह्मचारिन्, a novice under training for monkhood.

Caitra
(‘with Citrā’)
------------------------------------------
Caitra is the first month of the Hindu lunar चलेन्दर्, and roughly corresponds to March-April. It got its name from the fact that on the full-मोओन् day of that month, the मोओन् would be in the asterism Citrā. निरृति is the supervising deity of this month. Though Citrā is no longer connected with this month now, the name still continues as such.
The first day of this month is ‘Yugādi’ (the beginning of the yuga or Age), the New Year’s day, celebrated with religious vows and worship. The eighth day of the bright half is अशोकाष्टमी, a day on which goddess दुर्गा is worshipped with the flowers of the अशोक tree. Śrī राम-navamī, the birthday of the epic hero Śrī राम, is celebrated on the next day. In the dark fortnight, Matsya Jayantī (on the fifth day) and Varāha Jayantī (on the fourteenth day) are the important festivals.

caitya
(‘of the funeral pyre’)
------------------------------------------
‘Citā’ is the funeral pyre. ‘Caitya’ is anything that is connected with it. However in practice, a funeral mound, a tree with a rivetment round its stem probably interring the remains of a hero, or even a building serving the same purpose, have all been designated as caityas. The term has also been used as a general nomenclature for any temple.
Over the years the word has acquired a peculiarly Buddhistic flavour. Places—with or without a monument—such as Lumbiṇī, गया, Vaiśālī or Rājagṛha associated with बुद्ध’s life, have come to be known as caityas. Stūpas also have been called caityas.
In the rock-cut चवे तेम्प्लेस् of Buddhistic origin, चैत्य Halls are seen. They are apsidal, barrel-vaulted halls used to enshrine a stūpa.

Caitanya Mahāprabhu
